forces: Orchestra with piano, celesta and two harps
performers: Orchestre de la Suisse Romande; Ernest Ansermet
question: How do exposed instrumental lines change our sense of the puppet heard dancing with the others?
intro: Behind the puppet theatre, Petrushka’s music alternates violent gestures with exposed piano and wind lines. Two clarinets make the famous C-major/F♯-major clash sound like one character unable to settle into a single harmonic identity.

sections.label: Cries and curses
sections.mNote: opposed triads and piano figuration expand into orchestral outbursts

sections.label: An inward lament
sections.mNote: lighter wind and piano writing replaces the preceding weight

sections.label: The Ballerina’s visit
sections.mNote: animated gestures interrupt the more gently shaped wind lines

sections.label: Abandonment and despair
sections.mNote: fragmented gestures grow towards another orchestral cry

cues.title: Two triads, one character
cues.text: Petrushka’s signature sound sets C major against F♯ major. The two clarinet lines turn those familiar triads into an abrasive combined figure; the piano takes up the conflict rather than resolving it into one ordinary key.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 63–65, rehearsals 48–51, supplies the paired clarinets, piano and opposed triads. The report’s first quiet stretch contains prominent C, C♯, F♯ and G, then gains activity at 0:45–1:05. The cue describes the opening sequence, not its first clarinet note. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A room made of cardboard
cues.text: The original scenario gives Petrushka a black cardboard room painted with stars and a crescent moon. A portrait of the Charlatan hangs on the wall. His prison belongs visibly to a puppet theatre even while the music gives him human distress.
cues.evidence: Kirchmeyer, Summary, describes the second tableau’s scenery and the Charlatan’s portrait. https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: After the outburst
cues.text: The early orchestral cry collapses into much more exposed writing. In this inward passage, piano and high winds leave space around their gestures; compare the change of texture with the force of the preceding tutti.
cues.evidence: Score p. 67 moves from Furioso into Adagietto at rehearsal 52. The 1:12 boundary follows the 1:00–1:05 crest, with relative level falling to −24.6 dB at 1:15. This is a passage placement. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The ballet’s first nucleus
cues.text: In Stravinsky’s retrospective account, the music he played to Diaghilev became the second tableau. The idea of the puppet’s struggle therefore preceded the completed fairground setting: the piano was central before Petrushka became a danced role.
cues.evidence: IRCAM quotes Stravinsky identifying the piece played to Diaghilev as the future second tableau. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka

cues.title: Tenderness and awkward display
cues.text: Through the visit sequence, compare the more gently shaped flute-and-piano writing with the animated gestures that follow. Petrushka’s attempt at courtship does not acquire the smooth continuity of a conventional ballet duet.
cues.evidence: Score pp. 68–70 moves from Andantino through the Ballerina’s entrance to Allegro. Changes at 1:56 and 2:18 precede the rise at 2:45–3:00. The broad sequence is located; the Ballerina’s first step is not timed. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nijinsky’s puppet role
cues.text: Vaslav Nijinsky danced Petrushka at the Paris premiere on 13 June 1911; Tamara Karsavina was the Ballerina. Michel Fokine supplied the choreography, while Alexandre Benois designed the sets and costumes as well as helping devise the scenario.
cues.evidence: IRCAM’s work record gives the premiere date and production team; Kirchmeyer documents Benois’s scenario collaboration. https://resources.ircam.fr/en/work/petrouchka https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka

cues.title: Fragments gather force again
cues.text: After the visit, broken gestures begin to gather orchestral force again. Listen to the distance between quiet fragments and the later outburst: the scene repeatedly changes the size of Petrushka’s musical voice.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-room.txt: the 3:08 change leads to very low relative levels at 3:10–3:15, followed by a rise through 3:35–3:45. Rehearsals 59–61 supply the final despair sequence: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/179-k012-petrushka.

cues.title: No stable reconciliation
cues.text: The closing sequence withdraws from its outburst without giving Petrushka a comfortable harmonic reconciliation. The score recalls the paired clarinet gesture before the curtain music; carry that unresolved identity into the contrasting room of his rival.
cues.evidence: Score p. 77, rehearsal 61, includes a slow clarinet cadenza and curtain passage. Relative level retreats after 3:55, with a boundary at 4:04 and a darker spectral balance at 4:20–4:25. No final chord or drumstroke is aligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The orchestra releases its grip
transitions.how: The Furioso reaches held orchestral gestures and a pause; a piano glissando leads into Adagietto. Piano, high winds and xylophone replace the earlier weight of brass and strings. The opposing harmonic materials have not been reconciled: the sudden reduction in texture allows them to sound exposed rather than massed.
transitions.evidence: Score p. 67, rehearsal 52. The 1:12 measured boundary separates the crest at 1:00–1:05 from the low 1:15–1:30 interval. Piano glissando and instrumental assignments come from the score, not the audio features. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: A gentler line becomes an awkward display
transitions.how: After the flute and piano’s more gently shaped lines, the Ballerina’s entrance leads into Allegro. Sharply separated gestures and changing orchestral combinations replace the preceding continuity. The visit is framed by a change in pace and articulation, not by a cadence establishing a secure new home key.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 69–70, end of rehearsal 55 into 56, places the entrance before Allegro. The report’s 2:46 boundary and rise in attack density and level at 2:45–3:00 place that animated passage, rather than the earlier 2:18 change within its preparation. The first stage gesture remains unaligned. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

transitions.title: Courtship breaks back into isolated gestures
transitions.how: The Ballerina leaves, and Petrushka’s music loses its temporary public display. Piano figures and short wind calls separate before the orchestral forces gather again. Alternations of movement and hesitation make the join a broken continuation of his complaint, rather than the start of an unrelated slow movement.
transitions.evidence: Score pp. 73–77, rehearsals 58–61. The report’s 3:08 change and quiet 3:10–3:15 interval place the withdrawal; the later crest is at 3:45–3:55. This is not a bar alignment of the departure. https://vmirror.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/1/18/IMSLP472771-PMLP179431-PMLUS00370-Stravinsky_-_Petrushka_OrchScore.pdf

source.title: Stravinsky, Petrushka, 1911 orchestration; Édition Russe plate R.M.V. 127, Dover reprint
source.locator: Printed pp. 63–77, rehearsals 48–61. Public-domain score in the US, not the EU. Passage timings are provisional, guided by cache/analysis/stravinsky-petrushka-room.txt. Xylophone is grouped under percussion; active groups describe a passage, not every simultaneous note.

timeline.note: The opening ejection gives way to Petrushka’s paired clarinets and piano.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 63–64; opening active sound, with reduced level through 0:10–0:40.

timeline.note: Exposed clarinet figures and piano arpeggios carry the puppet’s complaint.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 64, rehearsal 49; boundary at 0:30, before the growth in activity at 0:45.

timeline.note: The Furioso spreads the complaint through a larger wind, brass and string texture.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 65–67, rehearsal 51; crest at 1:00–1:05 and boundary at 1:12.

timeline.note: Adagietto reduces the sound to piano, high winds and xylophone.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 67, rehearsal 52; 1:12 boundary and low relative level at 1:15–1:30.

timeline.note: Andantino and the following visit preparation place a gentler line over the piano.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 68–69, rehearsals 53–55; 1:56 boundary, before the changed balance at 2:18. Groups vary within the passage.

timeline.note: The visit’s Allegro spreads animated gestures across piano, winds, brass and strings.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 70–73, rehearsals 56–58; 2:46 change, attack density 4.4/s at 2:45, and increasing level towards 3:00. Combinations change within the passage.

timeline.note: After the visit, piano and short wind gestures begin the final complaint.
timeline.evidence: Score pp. 73–74, rehearsals 58–59; quiet interval at 3:10–3:15 after the 3:08 boundary.

timeline.note: The last withdrawal includes the clarinets’ slow cadenza before the curtain passage.
timeline.evidence: Score p. 77, rehearsal 61; relative-level retreat after 3:55 and boundary at 4:04. The list covers the changing closing combinations, not a continuous tutti.

fields.note: A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.
